references.label: Crit Care 2020 Brainstem
references.citation: Rocha S, et al. Brainstem: neglected in critical care? Review of brainstem anatomy, functional organisation and clinical syndromes. Crit Care. 2020;24:5.
references.excerpt: The brainstem contains the nuclei of cranial nerves III to XII, the ascending and descending long tracts (corticospinal, spinothalamic and medial lemniscus pathways), the reticular formation with the ascending reticular activating system, and the cardiorespiratory centres. Because long tracts and cranial nerve nuclei are packed closely together, small lesions produce characteristic crossed syndromes such as lateral medullary (Wallenberg) and medial medullary syndromes.

references.label: BJA Educ 2016 ANS
references.citation: Wehrwein EA, Orer HS, Barman SM. Overview of the anatomy, physiology, and pharmacology of the autonomic nervous system. Compr Physiol. 2016;6(3):1239-1278.
references.excerpt: The sympathetic division has short preganglionic neurones arising from the thoracolumbar spinal cord (T1-L2) that synapse in paravertebral or prevertebral ganglia, with long postganglionic noradrenergic fibres. The parasympathetic division has long preganglionic neurones arising from cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and the sacral segments S2-S4, synapsing in ganglia close to their target organs, with short postganglionic cholinergic fibres.

references.label: BJA Educ 2017 Diaphragm
references.citation: Kokatnur L, Rudrappa M, et al. The diaphragm: anatomy, physiology and clinical relevance. BJA Education. 2017;17(9):306-311.
references.excerpt: The diaphragm is the principal muscle of inspiration. It arises from the xiphoid process, the costal margin of the lower six ribs and costal cartilages, and the lumbar vertebrae via the right and left crura and the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments, inserting into a central tendon. Motor innervation is entirely from the phrenic nerves (C3-C5); the aortic hiatus lies at T12, the oesophageal hiatus at T10 and the caval foramen at T8.

references.label: BJA Educ 2015 Thoracic Duct
references.citation: Riquet M, Le Pimpec Barthes F. Surgical anatomy of the thoracic duct and lymphatics of the chest. In: Shields TW, ed. General Thoracic Surgery. Reviewed in: Nair SK, Petko M, Hayward MP. Aetiology and management of chylothorax in adults. Eur J Cardiothorac Surg. 2007;32(2):362-369.
references.excerpt: The thoracic duct arises from the cisterna chyli at the level of the second lumbar vertebra, enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus, ascends to the right of the aorta, crosses to the left at the level of the fifth thoracic vertebra and drains into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins. Injury results in chylothorax.

references.citation: Ferraro MC, Cashin AG, Wand BM, et al. Interventions for treating pain and disability in adults with complex regional pain syndrome: an overview of systematic reviews. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2023;6:CD009416.
references.excerpt: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) is a chronic pain condition that usually occurs in a limb following trauma or surgery. It is characterised by persisting pain that is disproportionate in magnitude or duration to the typical course of pain after similar injury. There is currently no consensus regarding the optimal management of CRPS, although a broad range of interventions have been described and are commonly used.

references.excerpt: There is low-quality evidence that perineural administration of dexamethasone as a local anaesthetic adjunct increases duration of analgesia by an average of 2 h compared with intravenous injection for interscalene brachial plexus block.
